q: 1. Segregation in concrete results in
explain: Segregation separates coarse aggregate, mortar, and water unevenly, which can cause honeycombing, porous layers, and surface scaling all at once depending on where separation occurs.

q: 2. The percentage of water for making a cement paste of normal consistency varies from
explain: The standard consistency of cement paste, determined by the Vicat apparatus, is typically achieved with water content in the range of about 35% to 50% by weight of cement.

q: 3. The internal friction between the ingredients of concrete is minimized by
explain: Internal friction in a concrete mix can be reduced through several means together: using coarser aggregates, adding more water for lubrication, and reducing surface area/texture of particles, hence all of these contribute.

q: 4. The strength of concrete increases with increase in
explain: Concrete strength benefits from a lower water-cement ratio, appropriately larger aggregate (up to a limit for better interlocking), and finer cement particles that hydrate faster, so all these factors together increase strength.

q: 5. The condition not applicable to water cement ratio law, is
options: internal moisture conditions on hydration continue till complete strength is gained
concrete specimens may be tested at any temperature
concrete specimens need be of same age
concrete specimens need be of same size
explain: The water-cement ratio law assumes standard curing conditions; testing specimens 'at any temperature' is not a valid assumption of the law, since temperature affects hydration and thus strength results.

q: 6. If the slump of a concrete mix is 60 mm, its workability is
explain: A slump value of 60mm falls within the medium workability range as per standard slump classification tables.

q: 7. Water cement ratio is generally expressed in volume of water required per
explain: Water-cement ratio is conventionally expressed as the volume/quantity of water required per standard 50 kg bag of cement.

q: 8. Excess quantity of water
explain: Too much water in a concrete mix promotes both segregation of the aggregate from the paste and bleeding (rise of water to the surface), so both b and c occur.

q: 9. Too wet concrete may cause
explain: An overly wet concrete mix can simultaneously cause reduced strength, excessive laitance formation at the surface, and segregation of the ingredients.

q: 10. The top diameter, bottom diameter and the height of a slump mould are
explain: The standard slump mould (frustum of a cone) as per IS 7320 has a top diameter of 10 cm, bottom diameter of 20 cm, and a height of 30 cm.

q: 11. Pick up the incorrect statement from the following:
options: the bottom and top ends of slump mould are parallel to each other
the axis of the mould is perpendicular to the end faces
the internal surface of the mould is kept clean and free from set cement
the mould is in the form of a frustum of hexagonal pyramid
explain: The slump mould is in the shape of a frustum of a cone (circular cross-section), not a hexagonal pyramid, making this statement incorrect.

q: 12. Slump test of concrete is a measure of its
explain: The slump test measures the consistency (workability/wetness) of fresh concrete, not any hardened property like strength.

q: 13. The strength of concrete made with angular aggregate and rounded aggregate is practically same at the water cement ratio of
explain: As per the data referenced in this text, at a water-cement ratio of about 0.48, the strength difference between angular and rounded aggregate concrete becomes negligible.

q: 14. The concrete having a slump of 6.5 cm, is said to be
explain: A slump of around 6.5 cm falls in the plastic concrete range, indicating good flowability suitable for normal placing and compaction.

q: 15. The slump for beam slab is
explain: For beams and slabs, a medium workability with a slump in the range of 50-100 mm is generally recommended for proper placement and compaction.

q: 16. The workability may be defined as the amount of applied work required to compact the concrete to its maximum density. The principle is used in
explain: The compaction factor test is based on the principle of determining the degree of compaction achieved by a standard amount of work done in dropping concrete through a standard height, directly relating to the definition given.

q: 17. Workability of concrete in which low water cement ratio is determined by
explain: The compaction factor test is more suitable and sensitive for measuring workability of stiff/low workability (low w/c ratio) mixes where the slump test is not effective.

q: 18. Pick up the correct statement from the following:
options: segregation is necessary for a workable concrete
consistency does not affect the workability of concrete
if the slump increases, workability decreases
if the concrete mix is dry, the slump is maximum
explain: None of the first four statements is technically correct: segregation is undesirable, consistency does affect workability, higher slump means higher (not lower) workability, and a dry mix gives minimum (not maximum) slump. Hence 'none of the above' is correct.

q: 19. The shrinkage of concrete
options: is proportional to water content is the mix
explain: Shrinkage in concrete is influenced together by the water content, cement content, and it accumulates further as the concrete ages, so all these factors are relevant.

q: 20. Pick up the correct statement from the following:
options: the quality of water governs the strength of concrete
the quality of water required for concreting, depends upon the grading of aggregate and method of compaction
10% excess of water reduces the strength of concrete by 15%
30% excess of water reduces the strength of concrete by 50%
explain: All these statements about the effect of water quality and excess water quantity on concrete strength are established facts in concrete technology, hence all are correct.

q: 21. For preparing ordinary concrete, the quantity of water used, is
options: 5% by weight of aggregates plus 20% of weight of cement
10% by weight of aggregates the plus 10% of weight of cement
5% by weight of aggregates plus of 30% weight of cement
30% by weight of aggregates plus 10% of weight of cement
explain: As a standard rule for ordinary concrete, water quantity is taken as approximately 5% of the weight of aggregates plus 30% of the weight of cement, providing a workable and practical mix.

q: 22. If P, Y and Z are the weights of cement, fine aggregates and coarse aggregates respectively and W/C is the water to be added to first batch, is obtained by the equation
explain: This is the standard empirical formula (0.3p + 0.1y + 0.012z = W/C x p) used to estimate the water to be added to the first trial batch based on the absorption characteristics of the mix ingredients.

q: 23. Water cement ratio by weight is
options: Higher as compared to that by volume
Lower is compared to that by volume
explain: Since cement is heavier than an equal volume of water, expressing the water-cement ratio by weight generally yields a higher numerical value compared to expressing it by volume.

q: 24. Shrinkage in concrete can be reduced by
options: Using tight and non-absorbent from work
explain: Shrinkage can be minimized through combined measures: reducing water-cement ratio, selecting suitable low-shrinkage aggregates, and using tight, non-absorbent formwork to retain moisture.

q: 25. The shrinkage of concrete is due to a change in
explain: Shrinkage fundamentally refers to a reduction in the overall volume of the concrete mass as it loses moisture over time.

q: 26. For a constant water cement ratio, decrease in aggregate cement ratio causes
explain: Reducing the aggregate-cement ratio (i.e., using proportionally more cement paste relative to aggregate) at a fixed water-cement ratio increases the paste content available to lubricate the mix, thereby increasing workability.

q: 27. Minimum water cement ratio required for fully hydration of cement is
explain: A water-cement ratio of about 0.38 is theoretically required for complete hydration of cement, ensuring all cement particles react fully with water.

q: 28. The percentage of water for making a cement paste of normal consistency varies from
explain: Typically, the water required to achieve standard/normal consistency of cement paste ranges from about 25% to 35% by weight of cement.

q: 29. The basic water demand depend on
explain: The basic water demand of a concrete mix is influenced together by the quality (nature, absorption) of the materials used and the target water-cement ratio.

q: 30. The minimum water-cement ratio to obtain workable concrete is
explain: A minimum water-cement ratio of about 0.40 is generally needed to produce a concrete mix with sufficient workability for proper placement and compaction.

q: 31. Internal friction between the ingredients of concrete, is decreased by using
explain: Using more water (which lubricates the mix) along with coarse aggregate (which has less surface area/friction compared to fine material) reduces the internal friction between the concrete ingredients.

q: 32. More water should not be added in the concrete mix so as to increase
explain: Adding extra water beyond the design mix raises the water-cement ratio, which in turn reduces strength and durability — so all of these are adversely affected.

q: 33. Workability of concrete is inversely proportional to
explain: As the time of transit increases, some water evaporates and initial hydration begins, causing the mix to stiffen - hence workability decreases (inversely proportional) with increasing transit time.

q: 34. For batching 1:3:6 and water cement ratio 0.6 both by weight, the quantity of water required per bag, is
explain: For a 50 kg cement bag with a water-cement ratio of 0.6 by weight, the water required = 0.6 x 50 = 30 kg.

q: 35. Water required per bag of cement is
explain: As a general rule referenced in this text, about 28 kg (litres) of water is required per 50 kg bag of cement for a typical nominal mix.

q: 36. The maximum water cement ratio in plain concrete to ensure durability in mild exposure is limited to
explain: For plain concrete under mild exposure conditions, the maximum permissible water-cement ratio specified for durability is 0.7.

q: 37. Steel mould used for slump test is in the form of :
explain: The standard slump test mould is a frustum of a cone (Abrams cone), which is filled with concrete and lifted vertically to measure the resulting slump.

q: 38. The strength of concrete increase with decreases in :
explain: Strength of concrete is inversely related to the water-cement ratio — as the water-cement ratio decreases, the paste becomes denser and strength increases (Abrams' law).
